intro: Four trees, and three of them are at Morris Arboretum. Bartram's Ginkgo, the oldest ginkgo in America, grows alone at Bartram's Garden on the Schuylkill, planted in 1785 by William Hamilton and outliving the two he kept for himself. Across town at Morris Arboretum stand a natural oak hybrid nobody bred, a katsura whose autumn leaves smell of brown sugar, and a weeping hemlock that survived a world's fair, a 1947 move, and the 2024 storm that killed its twin.
meta_description: Bartram's Ginkgo, America's oldest, grows by the Schuylkill. Three more at Morris Arboretum: a wild oak hybrid, a fragrant katsura, a weeping hemlock.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Philadelphia is Bartram's Ginkgo, growing east of the Bartram Barn at Bartram's Garden in Southwest Philadelphia, believed to be around 240 years old. It grew from a sapling William Hamilton shipped from London in 1785 and gave to his friend William Bartram, and it is thought to be the oldest ginkgo in North America. The garden is free and open every day, dawn to dusk. Three more trees are mapped at Morris Arboretum across town: a wild oak hybrid that may run nearly as old, a katsura whose autumn leaves smell of brown sugar, and a weeping hemlock that survived a 1947 move and the 2024 storm that killed its twin.
question_meta: Bartram's Ginkgo, planted 1785, roughly 240 years old, is Philadelphia's oldest tree and America's oldest ginkgo, one of four mapped here.
question_context:
The date rests on a specific claim rather than a general one. In 1785, William Hamilton of The Woodlands shipped three ginkgo saplings from London, the first of their kind to reach North America. He kept two at his own estate and gave the third to his friend William Bartram, whose garden on the Schuylkill was already the oldest botanic garden on the continent. Both of Hamilton's trees were cut down in the 1980s, leaving Bartram's the sole survivor and the oldest ginkgo known in the country. It is a male tree, sparing the garden the foul-smelling seed ginkgoes are known for. The garden is free, open every day, dawn to dusk, a 10 minute walk from the Woodland Avenue trolley.

Three more trees stand across town at Morris Arboretum, a paid garden: a Bender Oak hybrid nobody bred, possibly close to the ginkgo's own age; a katsura whose autumn leaves smell of brown sugar; and a weeping hemlock, moved to its current spot in 1947, that outlived a 2024 storm which killed its twin by the pond.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Philadelphia?
faq.a: Bartram's Ginkgo at Bartram's Garden, believed to be around 240 years old and the oldest ginkgo tree in North America.

faq.q: Why is it the oldest ginkgo in America?
faq.a: It is one of three saplings William Hamilton shipped from London in 1785. He kept two for his own estate, The Woodlands, and gave the third to his friend William Bartram. Hamilton's two were cut down in the 1980s; this is the only one left.

Yes. Bartram's Garden is a city-owned public garden and National Historic Landmark, free and open every day, dawn to dusk. Morris Arboretum, where the other three trees on this page stand, charges general admission.

The Woodland Avenue trolley (route 34) stops about a 10 minute walk from Bartram's Garden, and SEPTA bus routes 12 and 64 also serve Lindbergh Boulevard near the entrance. Morris Arboretum, in Chestnut Hill, is reached by the SEPTA Chestnut Hill West line to Allen Lane.

faq.q: What trees are at Morris Arboretum?
faq.a: Three on this page: the Bender Oak, a natural hybrid that happened on its own; the arboretum's signature Katsura, whose fallen leaves smell of brown sugar each October; and a weeping hemlock that survived the 1876 Centennial Exposition, a 1947 move, and the 2024 storm that took down its twin by the pond.

trees.name: Bartram's Ginkgo

location.address: Bartram's Garden, 5400 Lindbergh Blvd, Philadelphia, PA 19143 (east of the Bartram Barn)

trees.story:
In 1785, William Hamilton shipped three ginkgo saplings from London, the first of their kind to reach North America. He planted two at his own estate, The Woodlands, and gave the third to his friend William Bartram, whose garden a few miles up the Schuylkill was already the oldest botanic garden on the continent. Hamilton's two are gone, felled in the 1980s. Bartram's is the one that made it.

That leaves this tree, standing east of the old barn on the same ground Bartram himself planted, as the oldest ginkgo known in America at roughly 240 years old. It is male, which spares the garden a problem: ginkgoes are dioecious, and only the females drop the soft, foul-smelling seed that gives the species its reputation at street level. Whoever decided which sapling went where left Bartram with the tidier tree.

The 1785 date is well attested. Wikipedia and the garden's own institutional history agree closely on it, though both likely trace back to the same original record rather than two truly independent counts, worth knowing before treating the figure as beyond question. No exact coordinates for the trunk have ever been published, so the pin here marks the general area rather than the base of the tree itself.

Bartram's Garden is free, city owned, and open every day from dawn to dusk.
trees.access: Free, open to visitors every day, grounds open dawn to dusk (Welcome Center Thu-Mon 9:30am-4:30pm). Bartram's Garden is a city-owned public garden and National Historic Landmark; no ticket needed.
trees.transport: Woodland Ave trolley (route 34) to 54th St, then about a 10 minute walk; SEPTA bus routes 12/64 also serve Lindbergh Blvd near the garden entrance

best_time.label: November, when the whole crown turns gold and can drop within a day or two

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands, east of the old Bartram barn on the ground Bartram planted. It is a male tree, so it drops none of the foul seed a female ginkgo does.

trees.name: The Bender Oak
trees.species: Bender Oak, a natural hybrid of Scarlet Oak x Northern Red Oak (Quercus x benderi)

location.address: Morris Arboretum, 100 East Northwestern Avenue, Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia, PA 19118 (stop 1 of the Great Trees tour, near the historic hilltop mansion site)

trees.access: Paid entry at Morris Arboretum & Gardens (University of Pennsylvania): adults $22, seniors 65+ $20, youth 3 to 17 $12, children 2 and under free (prices as shown on the Arboretum's own site). Hours change with the season, so check the site before you go.
trees.transport: Chestnut Hill, northwest Philadelphia; SEPTA Chestnut Hill West line to Allen Lane, then about a 15-20 minute walk, or bus routes serving Northwestern Ave
trees.story:
Nobody bred this oak. It is a cross between a scarlet oak and a northern red oak that happened on its own, the kind of hybrid botanists did not even get round to naming until 1903, in Breslau. The one at Morris Arboretum may be up to 250 years old, which would put it at roughly the age of the United States. The arboretum's own guide says possibly; the lower end of the honest range is nearer 150.

It is also big in the way that matters: 26.5 metres tall, a trunk more than two metres across, and a canopy spreading over 30 metres. The Morris family, whose estate became the arboretum, had it as the dramatic entrance to their garden and their home on the hill. Today it is the first stop on the arboretum's own Great Trees tour.

There was once another notable Bender oak in the Philadelphia area, at Swarthmore College, reckoned at over 350 years. It was felled some time before 2009. This one is still standing, a hybrid most visitors have never heard of in a spot where they expect an ordinary oak.

It stands near the old mansion site at the start of the garden. Entry to the arboretum is paid. The pin is approximate; follow the Great Trees tour to stop one.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the spread, a canopy over 30 metres wide on a trunk more than two metres across. It stands at stop one of the arboretum's Great Trees tour, near the old hilltop mansion site.

trees.name: The Katsura-Tree of Morris Arboretum

location.address: Morris Arboretum, 100 East Northwestern Avenue, Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia, PA 19118 (stop 7 of the Great Trees tour)

trees.access: Paid entry at Morris Arboretum & Gardens (University of Pennsylvania): adults $22, seniors 65+ $20, youth 3 to 17 $12, children 2 and under free (prices as shown on the Arboretum's own site). Hours change with the season, so check the site before you go.
trees.transport: Chestnut Hill, northwest Philadelphia; SEPTA Chestnut Hill West line to Allen Lane, then about a 15-20 minute walk
trees.story:
Philadelphia Magazine once called this the largest tree in Philadelphia, which is a bold thing to say about a tree barely 120 years old. It is a katsura, native to Japan and China, planted around 1902 by the Morris family on the estate that became Morris Arboretum, and it has grown into one of the largest of its kind in North America.

The arboretum calls it its signature tree, and it earns the title in two ways. The first is plain size. The second arrives in autumn, when the leaves turn yellow and apricot and the air under the crown starts to smell of cinnamon and brown sugar, a bakery where you expected a garden.

In the century and a bit since it went in, the Morris estate around it has become a public garden run by the University of Pennsylvania, and a family planting has become the tree the arboretum puts forward as its emblem. It is stop seven on the arboretum's own Great Trees tour.

Entry to the arboretum is paid. The pin marks the arboretum rather than the tree, so follow the tour to stop seven, and in October let your nose help.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, unusual for a katsura, and in autumn by the yellow and apricot leaves that smell of brown sugar. It stands at stop seven of the arboretum's Great Trees tour.

best_time.label: October, when the leaves turn yellow and apricot and smell of brown sugar

trees.name: The Weeping Hemlock at the Meadowbrook Gate

location.address: Morris Arboretum, Meadowbrook Avenue gate, Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia, PA 19118

trees.access: Paid entry at Morris Arboretum & Gardens (University of Pennsylvania): adults $22, seniors 65+ $20, youth 3 to 17 $12, children 2 and under free (prices as shown on the Arboretum's own site). Hours change with the season, so check the site before you go.
trees.transport: Chestnut Hill, northwest Philadelphia; SEPTA Chestnut Hill West line to Allen Lane, then about a 15-20 minute walk
trees.story:
This weeping hemlock was a celebrity once. In 1876 it went on show at the Centennial Exposition in Fairmount Park, the world's fair that marked America's hundredth birthday, where the Parsons & Sons nursery exhibited weeping hemlocks and, by the arboretum's account, created a sensation among horticulturists.

Two of those exhibition hemlocks came to the Morris estate afterwards. One was planted near the pond. The other went in near the Key Fountain, and in 1947 it was dug up and moved to a new home at the Meadowbrook Avenue gate. Moving a tree of that age is a gamble. It worked.

The twin by the pond was not so lucky. On 13 February 2024 a wet, heavy snowstorm brought it down, and the arboretum wrote its obituary. If you are carrying the older printed Great Trees brochure, its stop eleven describes that pond tree, which is gone. The survivor is this one, at the gate.

It is a weeping form of the eastern hemlock, the branches falling rather than reaching, and at roughly 150 years, counted from its first public appearance in 1876, it has now outlived both its sister and the fair that made it famous.

Entry to the arboretum is paid. The pin is approximate; head for the Meadowbrook Avenue gate.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the weeping habit, branches hanging down rather than reaching out, on a hemlock that has stood here since 1947. It stands at the arboretum's Meadowbrook Avenue gate, not by the pond.

trees.name: The Bartram Yellowwood

location.address: Bartram's Garden, 5400 Lindbergh Blvd, Philadelphia, PA 19143 (Kitchen Garden, east of the Bartram House)

location_site.name: Bartram's Garden Kitchen Garden beside the house

trees.story:
In June 2010 a storm hit this yellowwood hard enough that the Inquirer wrote it up as news. It was already about two centuries old then, some 60 feet tall and 20 feet round at the middle, rotted and hollow inside, its branches held together with wire by the garden's staff. Lightning struck it; WHYY reported that the storm tore off six limbs and left one. The Inquirer put a full recovery at ten to twenty years away.

The garden now describes it as recovering, still growing and still blooming, and counts it among its oldest trees, presiding over the Kitchen Garden beside the Bartram House for more than 200 years.

How it got here is a good story with soft edges. The French plant explorer André Michaux recorded the species in central Tennessee in 1796, and the likeliest account has him gathering it there. The Inquirer has it reaching William Bartram around 1800; Wikipedia says it was possibly collected in 1796. Neither is a planting record, so the honest age is somewhere past 200 years, not a date.

It came to a garden that is now counted the oldest surviving botanic garden on the continent, and it has stood through every chapter since. A younger yellowwood grows a little farther east. This is the old one, the hollow, much-mended trunk by the house.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, old, hollow and much repaired, with wired branches. It stands in the Kitchen Garden just east of the Bartram House; the younger yellowwood farther east is not it.
trees.access: Free grounds at Bartram's Garden; Welcome Center open Thursday to Monday 9:30am to 4:30pm (garden page; admission not stated on that page, grounds are a public park)
trees.transport: Trolley route 11 to 49th St and Woodland Ave, or SEPTA bus 36 to 54th St and Lindbergh Blvd, then a short walk in; roughly 25 minutes from Center City
trees.verify_notes: One source (the garden itself, plus dated news). Garden says: one of the Garden's oldest trees, has reigned over the Kitchen Garden for more than 200 years; badly damaged in a wind storm in 2010 but recovering, still growing and blooming (garden page, undated). Origin: probably gathered in Tennessee by the French plant explorer Andre Michaux (garden: observed species in central Tennessee 1796), brought to William Bartram around 1800 per the Inquirer 2010; Wikipedia says possibly collected 1796. Dates conflict, do not sharpen. Inquirer 26 June 2010: struck by lightning, about two centuries old, 60 ft tall, 20 ft around at the middle, rotted and hollow inside, staff had wired branches together, regrowth estimated 10 to 20 years (girth 610 cm and height 18 m converted from those figures, 2010 values). WHYY 2010 says the storm tore off six limbs leaving one. A younger second yellowwood stands slightly farther east (Wikipedia citing Reid 2010), so identify the OLD one beside the Kitchen Garden by the hollow, wired trunk. Pin is the garden's Kitchen Garden area from description, not the trunk; OSM Overpass unreachable. Life: no dated trunk observation; garden page undated says alive; iNaturalist RECENT 2026-08-09 near garden only. trees.name: The Woodlands Champion Zelkova

location.address: The Woodlands, 4000 Woodland Ave, Philadelphia, PA 19104 (near the Hamilton Mansion)

location_site.name: The Woodlands, lawn around the Hamilton Mansion

trees.story:
The Woodlands once had seven champion English elms around its mansion. Dutch elm disease killed every one, the last by March 2017, and four dead snags still stand there. Their relative from the Caucasus is still alive near the same mansion, and the cemetery lists it as a Pennsylvania state champion.

This ground has a long record with trees. Before it was a cemetery it was William Hamilton's estate, the place where, in 1785, he planted two of the first ginkgoes to reach North America. The Hamilton Mansion still stands, and the zelkova grows near it. The cemetery's own tree page sets a recent photograph of it beside a 1920 picture of an earlier zelkova on the grounds, which says something about how long this species has been part of the place.

What nobody has published is a measurement or an age. No girth, no height, no planting year appears in any source we found, and even the count of champions here varies. The cemetery speaks of fifteen, a TreePhilly tour of six. Penn Today, in 2012, named the zelkova alongside an English elm and a hedge maple as the cemetery's record holders. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

The Woodlands is free during posted gate hours, a short trolley ride from Center City.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it from the recent photograph on the cemetery's tree page. It stands on the grounds beside the Hamilton Mansion, and the cemetery's tree finder places it.
trees.access: Free; cemetery grounds open to visitors during posted gate hours (check The Woodlands visit page for current hours)
trees.transport: Trolley routes 11, 13, 34, 36 to 40th St and Woodland Ave, or 15 minutes on foot from Penn; roughly 15 minutes from Center City

best_time.label: October, when the whole crown turns orange-brown

trees.verify_notes: Owner's page (The Woodlands tree page) lists a State Champion Caucasian Zelkova near the Hamilton Mansion with a recent photo, and a 1920 photo of an earlier zelkova on the grounds. Penn Today 2012 lists the cemetery's champions as an English elm, a hedge maple and a Caucasian zelkova. A TreePhilly champion-tree event page mentions a tour of six state champions including the historic zelkova. No girth or height found on any fetched page; champion year not shown. A tree-care company blog says it may descend from a tree planted in the 1700s by William Hamilton: one unreliable source, unverified, do not state. Sister champions: the seven English elms near the mansion all died of Dutch elm disease by March 2017 (owner), four snags remain; not delivered. The cemetery says 'fifteen' champions elsewhere vs TreePhilly 'six': counts disagree. Pin is the mansion area (wiki coordinate for the site), not the trunk. Life: owner page shows a recent photo; iNaturalist RECENT 2026-04-20 within the site. recognise: the zelkova on the grounds beside the Hamilton Mansion, find it via the cemetery's tree finder / tree page. Photo identity not found (not searched deeply).

trees.name: The Laurel Hill Cutleaf Linden

location.address: Laurel Hill Cemetery East, 3822 Ridge Ave, Philadelphia, PA 19132 (Section T, tag 473)

trees.story:
The cut-leaf form of the bigleaf linden is supposed to stay small. This one did not. Laurel Hill Cemetery calls it the second-largest bigleaf linden in Pennsylvania, counting the ordinary species too, and the state champion among cut-leaf trees.

The cultivar is the European bigleaf linden with its leaves remade. Where the species has a plain heart-shaped leaf, this one is irregularly lobed and cut, so the foliage looks snipped and shredded. It is normally a much smaller tree than the species it comes from. Somebody planted this one in Section T of Laurel Hill East, among the graves, and it kept growing until the cemetery put it on its list of notable trees.

That list is the only source for it, and it gives no girth, no height and no planting date. So the size claim is the cemetery's own, unmeasured as far as we can find, and the tree's age is an open question. If you know when it went in, or have measured it, tell us.

Laurel Hill is large and the pin marks the cemetery, not the trunk. Go to Section T and look for tag 473, and for those ragged leaves. Entry is free; the gates open at 7am.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, irregularly lobed and cut so they look shredded, and by its tag, number 473. It stands in Section T of Laurel Hill East.
trees.access: Free; cemetery gates open 7am to 7pm spring to fall and 7am to 5pm fall to spring (owner page)
trees.transport: SEPTA bus 61 or 35 to Ridge Ave and Huntingdon St, short walk; roughly 30 minutes from Center City
trees.verify_notes: One source, the owner (Laurel Hill Cemetery arboretum notable-trees page): tag 473, Section T, Laurel Hill East; 'second-largest bigleaf linden in the state'; 'State Champion cut-leaf cultivar'; the cultivar is usually much smaller than the species. No girth, height or age on the page. Pin is only the cemetery coordinate (wiki), trunk not placed; cemetery map section T / tag 473 needed for the exact spot. Not a small site: cemetery is large, so no location_site. Findability depends on a recognition clue: irregularly lobed, cut or shredded looking leaves, tag 473, Section T. Life: owner page current; iNaturalist RECENT 2026-07-06 within the cemetery only. The weeping beech (tag 2338) and weeping pagoda tree (tag 758) are champions at Laurel Hill West in Bala Cynwyd, outside the city, not delivered.

trees.name: The Hobson Street Scholar Tree

location.address: Hobson St across from Buist Park, 2526 Hobson St, Philadelphia, PA 19142

trees.story:
On Hobson Street the sidewalk bends out into the road to go round this tree, and the street gave up a parking space to let it. Philadelphia Parks & Recreation says the tree survived several development projects, and the neighbourhood was planned around it rather than the other way round. It is a scholar tree, also sold as the Japanese pagoda tree, though it is native to China.

How big is it? A blog's list of Philadelphia's notable trees gives 88 feet tall and 15.5 feet round, about 27 metres and 4.7 metres, and calls it the Pennsylvania champion of its species. That list is a pointer rather than an official register, and we could not confirm either the figures or the title anywhere else, so treat them as a good reason to go and look rather than a fact. Nobody has published its age. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

The Parks department chose it in 2021 as one of five notable trees worth seeking out in the city. It stands across from Buist Park in Elmwood, a public street tree you see from the sidewalk. Come in August, when it flowers in cream panicles while almost nothing else does.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the sidewalk, which curves out round its base and takes a parking space from the street. It stands on Hobson Street opposite Buist Park.
trees.access: Free; public street tree, view from the sidewalk
trees.transport: SEPTA trolley 36 to Elmwood Ave and 70th St area, a short walk; roughly 30 minutes from Center City

best_time.label: August, when cream flowers cover the crown in late summer

trees.verify_notes: One source, the owner (Philadelphia Parks & Recreation, 15 Dec 2021): on Hobson Street across from Buist Park (2526 Hobson St); survived several development projects, the neighbourhood was planned around it, and the sidewalk curves out around its base, taking a parking space. Size figures 88 ft tall and 15.5 ft circumference (converted: 27 m, 472 cm) come only from the finding aid phillytrees.blogspot.com Notable Trees List, which calls it the Pennsylvania champion on Hobson St between 67th and 68th Sts; not a source, so figures are unconfirmed and champion status unconfirmed. trees.name: The Washington Square Sycamore

location.address: 6th Street edge of Washington Square, 225 S 6th St, Philadelphia, PA 19106

trees.story:
The famous sycamore of Washington Square is gone. The one worth walking to stands just outside the wall, on the 6th Street sidewalk, and Philadelphia Parks & Recreation calls it likely the largest sycamore in Center City.

The famous one was the square's Moon Tree, a sycamore planted in 1975 from seed that had travelled to the Moon. It died, a clone of it died too, and the clone was removed in 2019. Only a plaque remains. The big sycamore on the sidewalk outlived both.

Washington Square has had shade trees since a planting programme began in 1816, but no source ties this trunk to that date. The Parks department gives no measurement and no age. All it says is that this is probably the biggest of its kind in the middle of the city, which, among the brick and the traffic, is a fair thing to be. If you know how old it is, tell us.

American sycamores give themselves away at a distance. The bark flakes off in patches, and the upper trunk and branches turn pale, almost white, above the darker base. In winter, bare, that pale frame is easy to pick out from the end of the block.

It is free, on a public sidewalk, open at all hours, a short walk from the Walnut-Locust stations.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, the biggest sycamore along this side of the square, with pale flaking bark. It stands on the 6th Street sidewalk just outside the wall of Washington Square.
trees.access: Free; public sidewalk at the square, open at all times
trees.transport: SEPTA Walnut-Locust (Broad-Ridge Spur or Market-Frankford) stations, about a 5 to 10 minute walk; in Center City
trees.verify_notes: One source, the owner (Philadelphia Parks & Recreation, 15 Dec 2021): along 6th Street just outside the walls of Washington Square; 'likely the largest sycamore in Center City'; no measurements or age given.
